Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- The UK government has clashed with the judiciary amid claims that Washington pressured London into not releasing documents that reveal the torture of a terrorism suspect, UK media report. Binyam Mohamed has been held at Guantanamo Bay for more than four years. Ethiopian Binyam Mohamed, 30, formerly resident in the UK, has been held at Guantanamo Bay since September 2004. Allegations that he he was involved in a plot to release a "dirty bomb" in the United States have now been withdrawn. Mohamed and his supporters allege he was tortured in Pakistan, Morocco and Afghanistan between 2002 and 2004, and that the UK security services were complicit. UK media outlets had appealed against an earlier ruling to withhold documents relating to the alleged torture. Two UK High Court judges said Wednesday, in comments reported by the UK's Press Association, that the papers would still not be disclosed after UK foreign minister David Miliband warned their publication might affect intelligence sharing between the U.S. and UK. In their ruling, reported by PA, the judges said the documents included information "relevant to allegations of torture," but added that they did not contain any sensitive intelligence. Rather, the judges concluded, the material was "politically embarrassing" and urged the new U.S. administration to take a different approach. The judges also suggested the U.S. government had pressured London about the intelligence-sharing relationship should the documents be released. Miliband told the UK's Channel 4 News Wednesday that intelligence co-operation between nations relied on confidentiality and that there would have been repercussions if the papers had been released. But he added: "There has been no threat from the United States to 'break off' intelligence cooperation." "In this case, the United States made clear, in documents that have been published, that there would inevitably be serious and lasting harm if that fundamental principle was breached," Miliband said.  "It is American information and it is for the Americans to decide when to publish their information."  The UK government has peviously pressed for the release of Mohamed. Last month U.S. President Barack Obama set a one-year deadline for the closure of Guantanamo. Clive Stafford Smith, lawyer for Mohamed, said in a statement on the Web site of human rights group Reprieve that the U.S. and the UK governments were legally obliged to investigate any allegations of torture. "For the foreign secretary to give in to these illegal demands by the Bush Administration is capitulation to blackmail, pure and simple. It is hardly Britain's finest hour. As the judges say, it is up to President Obama to put his money where his mouth is. He must repudiate his predecessor's reprehensible policy." Earlier this week Miliband met with his U.S. counterpart, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton for talks in Washington. Clinton told media after her meeting that the U.S.-UK relationship stood the test of time, adding: "Our two countries have stood side by side confronting global challenges for a very long time. We share fundamental values and important fundamental objectives."

Mohamed, a 30-year-old Ethiopian who previously lived in Britain, has been detained at Guantanamo Bay since September 2004—more than four years. Claims that he participated in a plan to detonate a radioactive “dirty bomb” in the United States have since been dropped.

Mohamed and those supporting him say he was tortured in Pakistan, Morocco and Afghanistan from 2002 to 2004, with British intelligence agencies allegedly playing a role.

British news organizations challenged an earlier decision preventing the release of documents connected to those accusations. However, two High Court judges said Wednesday that the material would remain secret, the UK’s Press Association reported. Their decision followed a warning from Foreign Secretary David Miliband that publication could damage intelligence cooperation between Britain and the United States.

According to PA’s account of the ruling, the judges said the documents contained material “relevant to allegations of torture” but no sensitive intelligence. They characterized the information instead as “politically embarrassing” and called on the new U.S. administration to adopt a different position.

The judges also indicated that Washington had put pressure on London by raising concerns about the future of intelligence sharing if the documents became public.

Speaking to Britain’s Channel 4 News on Wednesday, Miliband said international intelligence partnerships depend on confidentiality and that releasing the papers would have had consequences. Nevertheless, he stated: “There has been no threat from the United States to ‘break off’ intelligence cooperation.”

“In this case, the United States made clear, in documents that have been published, that there would inevitably be serious and lasting harm if that fundamental principle was breached,” Miliband said. “It is American information and it is for the Americans to decide when to publish their information.”

The British government has previously called for Mohamed to be freed. Last month, U.S. President Barack Obama ordered that Guantanamo Bay be closed within one year.

Mohamed’s attorney, Clive Stafford Smith, said in a statement posted on the website of the human rights organization Reprieve that both the U.S. and British governments had a legal duty to investigate all torture allegations.

“For the foreign secretary to give in to these illegal demands by the Bush Administration is capitulation to blackmail, pure and simple. It is hardly Britain’s finest hour. As the judges say, it is up to President Obama to put his money where his mouth is. He must repudiate his predecessor’s reprehensible policy.”

Earlier in the week, Miliband traveled to Washington for discussions with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. After the meeting, Clinton told reporters that the longstanding U.S.-UK partnership had endured over time.

“Our two countries have stood side by side confronting global challenges for a very long time,” she said. “We share fundamental values and important fundamental objectives.”

counterfactuals.output:
## UK refuses to release Binyam Mohamed documents, citing U.S. intelligence concerns

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — The British government has refused to release documents concerning the alleged torture of former Guantanamo Bay detainee Binyam Mohamed, arguing that disclosure could damage intelligence cooperation with the United States.

The disputed material includes a summary of U.S. intelligence relating to Mohamed’s treatment while he was held overseas. Mohamed, an Ethiopian-born former British resident, says he was tortured during detention in Pakistan and Morocco before being transferred to the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

British officials have denied attempting to conceal evidence of mistreatment. They say the information was supplied by Washington on the understanding that it would remain confidential and warn that releasing it without U.S. consent could restrict future intelligence sharing.

The case has fueled claims that the United States pressured Britain to keep the documents secret. Government lawyers have cited concerns that disclosure could harm the longstanding intelligence relationship between the two countries, though U.S. officials have disputed suggestions that Washington issued a direct threat.

Civil liberties groups and Mohamed’s attorneys argue that national security should not be used to suppress evidence of possible torture or British knowledge of his treatment. They say the public has a right to know whether UK agencies were aware of, or indirectly involved in, abuses committed during U.S.-led counterterrorism operations.

Mohamed was arrested in Pakistan in 2002 and later transferred through a network of overseas detention facilities. He says he was subjected to severe abuse, including during detention in Morocco. The United States did not prosecute him, and he was released from Guantanamo and returned to Britain in 2009.

The controversy has placed the British government under growing pressure to explain what its intelligence agencies knew and whether information supplied by UK officials contributed to Mohamed’s interrogation.

Ministers maintain that Britain does not condone torture and that any allegations of wrongdoing should be investigated. Critics, however, say the refusal to publish the material undermines those assurances and prevents full public scrutiny of the case.

counterfactuals.output:
# British judges and David Miliband clash over secret Binyam Mohamed intelligence

**LONDON —** A dispute between senior British judges and Foreign Secretary David Miliband over the suppression of intelligence concerning former Guantánamo detainee Binyam Mohamed has placed the United Kingdom’s courts, ministers and intelligence-sharing relationship with the United States under intense scrutiny.

At the centre of the conflict were seven short paragraphs summarising information supplied by US authorities to British intelligence officers in 2002. Mohamed’s lawyers argued that the material supported his claim that British officials knew he was being subjected to cruel and abusive interrogation while held in Pakistan.

The government resisted publication, contending that disclosure of intelligence received from Washington would breach the long-established “control principle,” under which information supplied by one country may not be released by another without permission. Miliband also warned that publication could damage intelligence cooperation with the United States and, as a result, threaten national security.

Two High Court judges, Lord Justice Thomas and Mr Justice Lloyd Jones, became increasingly critical of that position. Their judgments raised questions not only about Mohamed’s treatment, but also about whether ministers had accurately described the likely American response to a court-ordered disclosure.

## Allegations of mistreatment

Mohamed, an Ethiopian-born British resident, was arrested in Pakistan in April 2002. He alleged that he was interrogated there before being secretly transferred to Morocco, where he said he was tortured, including being cut with a razor or scalpel. He was later held at the US-run prison at Bagram in Afghanistan and then transferred to Guantánamo Bay.

The United States did not accept all of Mohamed’s claims about his detention history and treatment. British proceedings, however, focused partly on what UK agencies knew about his treatment in Pakistan and whether information supplied by British officials contributed to his questioning.

An officer from the British Security Service, MI5, interviewed Mohamed in Pakistan in May 2002. British authorities subsequently passed questions and other information to the United States. Mohamed’s lawyers argued that the government possessed documents that could assist his defence before a US military commission and corroborate his allegations of abuse.

The US case against him was eventually abandoned, and Mohamed returned to Britain in February 2009 after nearly seven years in custody. He was not charged with a criminal offence in the United Kingdom.

## The seven paragraphs

In 2008, the High Court reviewed extensive classified material held by the British government. The judges prepared seven paragraphs that summarised what US authorities had told British intelligence about Mohamed’s detention and interrogation.

Although the paragraphs originated from American intelligence reports, they did not reveal the names of agents, operational techniques or intelligence sources in the conventional sense. They described Mohamed’s treatment while in custody, including interrogation methods that the judges later said could readily be characterised as cruel, inhuman or degrading.

The court initially withheld the passages after Miliband issued public-interest immunity certificates. The foreign secretary argued that publication, even by judges rather than ministers, would violate the control principle and could lead the United States to reconsider the intelligence it shared with Britain.

Miliband repeatedly insisted that he was not seeking to conceal evidence of wrongdoing. His position was that the protection of intelligence-sharing relationships was itself a vital national-security interest.

“The issue is not whether the government condones torture,” his case maintained in substance. “The issue is whether Britain can unilaterally disclose material supplied in confidence by an ally.”

## Judges question an American “threat”

The controversy intensified in February 2009 when Thomas and Lloyd Jones said they had been persuaded to redact the paragraphs partly because the United States had warned that disclosure could affect intelligence cooperation.

Their ruling was widely interpreted as saying Washington had threatened to reduce or cut intelligence sharing with Britain if the court published the material.

That suggestion caused political alarm. Intelligence exchanges between the two countries cover terrorism, military operations and threats to public safety. Any significant restriction could have serious consequences for Britain’s security agencies.

Miliband challenged the idea that the United States had issued a blanket threat. He said there was no reason to believe Washington would stop sharing all intelligence with the United Kingdom. The concern, he argued, was narrower: the disclosure of US-originated material without consent could lead American agencies to restrict the particular categories of information they were willing to provide.

The distinction became a central point of friction. The judges said the government’s evidence had left them with the clear understanding that intelligence cooperation could be reconsidered. Ministers and officials, however, objected to language suggesting that Britain had been explicitly threatened with a broad intelligence shutdown.

The court subsequently examined a letter from the US State Department setting out Washington’s objections to disclosure. The judges said the correspondence showed that the United States would review the intelligence-sharing relationship if the passages were released. Critics of the government argued that this amounted to pressure on an independent court, regardless of whether it was formally described as a “threat.”

## Accusations of secrecy and possible complicity

Human-rights groups and Mohamed’s legal team accused the government of invoking national security to prevent public examination of possible British involvement in abuse.

They argued that the control principle could not be absolute, particularly where the material concerned alleged torture or cruel treatment. They also noted that substantial details about Mohamed’s interrogation had already emerged through legal proceedings and documents in the United States.

The government denied that it was trying to cover up mistreatment. Miliband said Britain opposed torture and did not ask other countries to use it. Ministers also stressed that allegations against intelligence personnel should be investigated through lawful procedures rather than decided by selective publication of classified documents.

The judges nevertheless expressed serious concern about the conduct of British authorities. They concluded that MI5 knew Mohamed had been held incommunicado and subjected to treatment that breached standards British officers were expected to observe.

Later disclosures indicated that Mohamed had been subjected in Pakistan to sleep deprivation, threats and prolonged shackling, and that his treatment had caused significant suffering. The court said the information was relevant to a public debate about the accountability of the security services.

## Press freedom enters the case

The legal battle widened when a group of British and international news organisations sought disclosure of the seven paragraphs. They argued that the public had a strong interest in learning what the government knew about the treatment of a British resident held overseas.

Media lawyers also said the information had already entered the public domain through US litigation. Once substantially similar material had been disclosed abroad, they argued, continued secrecy in Britain was difficult to justify.

The judges increasingly accepted that argument. They noted that a US federal court had made findings about Mohamed’s treatment and that the factual substance of the suppressed passages was no longer genuinely secret.

The government continued to warn, however, that the sensitivity lay not only in the underlying facts but in the official confirmation that US intelligence had supplied them to Britain. In intelligence diplomacy, ministers argued, official acknowledgment can carry consequences even when similar allegations are already publicly known.

## Court of Appeal orders disclosure

The dispute reached a decisive stage in February 2010, when the Court of Appeal ruled that the seven paragraphs should be published.

The court concluded that the material was essential to public understanding of Mohamed’s treatment and of the role played by British officials. It also took account of the fact that related information had been placed on the public record in the United States.

The released summary said Mohamed had been subjected to treatment including sleep deprivation, threats and shackling. It stated that the reported treatment, if administered in the United Kingdom, would have breached legal prohibitions and could be described as cruel, inhuman and degrading.

The ruling did not establish that British officers had personally tortured Mohamed. It did, however, deepen concerns that UK agencies had continued cooperating with US interrogators despite indications that he was being mistreated.

The Court of Appeal proceedings generated a further dispute when the judges criticised the Security Service’s record on candour. After submissions from government lawyers, part of that criticism was revised, prompting accusations that officials had attempted to soften judicial findings. The final judgment still raised significant questions about MI5’s handling of the case.

## Lasting implications

The Mohamed litigation became a landmark confrontation over the balance between open justice and national security. It tested how far ministers could rely on the intelligence control principle when courts believed disclosure was necessary to expose possible wrongdoing.

For Miliband, the case involved protecting a relationship that British governments regarded as indispensable. For the judges, it raised a constitutional question: whether foreign intelligence agencies, through warnings about future cooperation, could effectively determine what a British court was permitted to publish.

The affair also contributed to broader investigations into the alleged involvement of British agencies in the rendition and mistreatment of terrorism suspects after the September 11 attacks.

Mohamed later brought a civil claim against the British government. In November 2010, the government announced a confidential financial settlement with him and several other former Guantánamo detainees, without admitting liability.

The seven paragraphs ultimately revealed no intelligence source or covert operation. Their significance was instead institutional: they showed how information about a detainee’s treatment had moved between allied governments and how fiercely ministers resisted its disclosure.

The clash left unresolved tensions that continue to shape national-security litigation—between the promises governments make to intelligence partners, the duty of courts to administer justice openly and the public’s right to know whether state agencies were connected to serious human-rights abuses.

**British court disclosure fuels torture-complicity claims in Binyam Mohamed case**

**LONDON —** A British court ruling ordering the disclosure of previously secret intelligence in the case of former Guantánamo Bay detainee Binyam Mohamed has renewed allegations that British officials knew of, and may have been complicit in, his mistreatment while he was held in U.S. custody.

The disputed material—seven paragraphs summarizing reports supplied to Britain by U.S. intelligence—described Mohamed’s treatment during detention in Pakistan in 2002. Judges said the conduct included prolonged sleep deprivation, threats and other coercive measures that amounted, at a minimum, to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.

Mohamed, an Ethiopian-born former British resident, was arrested in Pakistan and later transferred through Morocco and Afghanistan before being sent to the U.S. detention camp at Guantánamo Bay. He alleges that he was tortured during that period, including being cut with a scalpel while held in Morocco. The United States did not prosecute him, and he returned to Britain in February 2009.

The litigation centered on whether the British public should be allowed to see what the government knew about Mohamed’s treatment. The High Court initially withheld the paragraphs after then-Foreign Secretary David Miliband argued that publication could damage intelligence cooperation with the United States. Subsequent rulings favored disclosure, concluding that the information was already known to U.S. authorities and that there was a strong public interest in revealing evidence of serious mistreatment.

The case also intensified scrutiny of the Security Service, MI5. A British officer questioned Mohamed in Pakistan, and his lawyers alleged that British agencies continued to provide information or questions despite knowing that he was being held in abusive conditions. British authorities have denied authorizing or condoning torture.

Miliband said the judgment did not establish that Britain had engaged in torture or become complicit in it. He maintained that the government had sought to protect the longstanding principle that intelligence supplied by an ally should not be disclosed without that ally’s consent. Britain, he said, remained firmly opposed to torture, although he warned that court-ordered publication could affect future intelligence sharing.

Clive Stafford Smith, Mohamed’s lawyer and the founder of the legal organization Reprieve, welcomed the disclosure as a victory for accountability. He said the material demonstrated that British officials had received clear information about Mohamed’s abuse and argued that the government’s efforts to keep it secret had delayed a proper examination of official conduct.

Stafford Smith called for a wider investigation into Britain’s role in U.S.-led detention and rendition operations after the September 11 attacks, saying the case raised questions beyond the actions of any single intelligence officer.

The ruling placed further pressure on the government to explain when ministers and intelligence officials first learned of Mohamed’s treatment and what steps, if any, they took in response. It also exposed tensions between national-security secrecy, Britain’s intelligence relationship with Washington and the courts’ responsibility to address credible allegations of torture.
